opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic reason is that there's nothing magical about human bodies or human hands. We're physical systems, and robots are physical systems. The things that have held robotics back historically are mostly not hardware problems. We've had pretty capable robotic hardware for a while: arms that are more precise than human arms, stronger, more tireless. What's been missing is the brain. The control software just hasn't been good enough to handle the messiness of the real world: picking up an unfamiliar object, folding laundry, working on a cluttered construction site.

So if you imagine superintelligent AI, systems that are better than the best humans at basically every cognitive task, then one of those cognitive tasks is "figure out how to control a robot body really well." And another is "design better robot bodies." And another is "design the factories that build the robots." Those are all fundamentally intellectual problems: engineering, design, control theory, learning from data. A superintelligence would be really good at them.

There's also an existence proof that this is doable at all: humans are able to do it with a few pounds of brain running on about twenty watts. You can take a human, put them in a body they've never had before, like a remote-controlled excavator, and after some practice they become quite skilled. Teleoperated robots today can already do a surprising amount of useful physical work when a human is the one steering. So the gap is really just replacing that human operator with an AI that's as good or better, and superintelligence by definition clears that bar.

And then there's the scale argument. Once you have one robot that can do a task, you can copy the software instantly to a million robots. The bottleneck becomes manufacturing, and we have enormous manufacturing capacity: the car industry alone produces tens of millions of vehicles a year. If you repurpose some of that capacity under the direction of superintelligent planners, I think you could get to very large numbers of capable robots surprisingly fast, maybe a year or a few years, not decades.

I'll caveat that there's real uncertainty about the exact speed. Physical stuff has friction that pure software doesn't: supply chains, permitting, building factories. But the question of *whether* robots controlled by superintelligent AI could do the physical work humans do, I think the answer is pretty clearly yes. The more interesting questions are how fast, and who's in control when it happens.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic case is pretty simple. Humans can do all this physical work, and we're not magical. Our bodies are machines, and our brains are the controllers of those machines. So in principle, there's no reason why you couldn't build a robot body that's roughly as dextrous and capable as a human body, and then have an AI controlling it that's at least as good as a human brain at controlling it.

And the thing is, the hardware side of this isn't actually that far off. Robot hands exist. Robot legs exist. They're a bit clunky and a bit expensive right now, but the main bottleneck for a long time has really been the software, the control problem. Robots were bad at manipulation not because the arms couldn't physically make the motions, but because the control systems weren't good enough to figure out what motions to make in messy, unstructured real-world environments.

And that's exactly the thing that superintelligence would solve. If you have AIs that are better than the best human engineers at everything, including robotics research, then they can do the research to close whatever remaining gaps there are in the hardware, and they can do the learning needed to actually control those bodies well. They can also run enormous amounts of simulation, and they can learn from huge fleets of robots in parallel, so the whole process of getting good at a physical task is much faster than it is for a human apprentice.

So then the question becomes less "can they do it?" and more "how fast does it scale up?" And that's where you get into the question of factories, supply chains, how many robots per year you can produce and so on. My guess is it'd be slow at first and then ramp up very quickly, because once the robots can help build more robots and more factories, you've got a feedback loop. It's a bit like how industrial economies grew, just much, much faster, because the thing that's doing the work doesn't need to be born and raised and trained for twenty years.

But to be clear, I'm not saying this happens overnight. The intelligence part might happen quite fast, and then the physical rollout lags behind that by some number of years. That lag is actually a pretty important part of how I think about the scenarios.

r004.rationale: It says superintelligent AI could conduct robotics research, close hardware gaps, and improve robot control and learning, accelerating progress.

astra-6.text:
Well, human beings are an existence proof that you can do all this physical work with a brain controlling a body. So the question is: what would prevent a superintelligent AI from controlling a robotic body at least as well?

There are real hardware challenges. You need sufficiently good sensors, actuators, batteries, and so on. Being superintelligent doesn’t magically make those constraints disappear. But a lot of what makes robotics difficult is getting the system to understand its surroundings and respond appropriately to unfamiliar situations. That’s something you’d expect a superintelligent system to be very good at. And it could also help design better hardware.

So I wouldn’t expect every human job to be automated the instant you get superintelligence. You still have to build and deploy the robots. But I don’t see a fundamental reason why the physical work humans do would remain beyond their capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, humans are an existence proof that it’s possible to do all this physical work with a body controlled by a brain. And our brains have pretty severe constraints on their size, energy consumption, and how quickly they can learn. So I don’t see a principled reason why an artificial system couldn’t do the same things, and eventually do them much better.

That doesn’t mean you get capable robots the instant you get superintelligent software. You still have to design the hardware, manufacture it, and deploy it. But a superintelligence could help enormously with those steps, including figuring out how to control bodies that are awkward or unreliable. So there might be a lag, but I wouldn’t expect physical work to remain a permanent human advantage.
